logCheckpoint.format: <tag> NUL <anchoringFormatVersion> NUL <32 raw blinding-nonce bytes> <canonical JSON of { checkpoint, signature }>

trustRegistry.format: <tag> NUL <anchoringFormatVersion> NUL <32 raw blinding-nonce bytes> <canonical JSON of { manifest, signatures }>

domainSeparation.note: The header is UTF-8 text and the nonce is 32 RAW bytes, not text. No separator follows the nonce because its width is fixed by this format. The two tags are why a checkpoint anchor can never be re-read as a registry anchor: see the deterministic layer, where one subject under two nonces already gives unrelated imprints.

howTheseWereProduced.twoLayers: Deterministic material — subjects, blinding nonces, anchorInput lengths and digests, and imprints — must be reproduced BYTE FOR BYTE by any runtime. Receipt material must be read or refused IDENTICALLY, with the same reason code.
howTheseWereProduced.blindingNonces: The blinding nonces here are fixed (0x00..0x1f and 0x20..0x3f) BECAUSE these are vectors and a vector must be reproducible. A deployment generates each blinding nonce from a cryptographically secure source and never regenerates it for a retry. A fixed nonce in production would defeat the property the nonce exists for.
howTheseWereProduced.subjects: The subjects are copies of already-published vectors: checkpoint-1 from evidence-log/v1/golden-vectors.json and document v1 from trust-registry/v1/golden-vectors.json. No new identifier is introduced, and no real tenant, action or payload identifier appears anywhere — none can, because neither admissible subject has a member to carry one.
howTheseWereProduced.receipts: The tokens are real RFC 3161 timestamp tokens obtained from a public timestamp authority over the published imprints. They embed the authority certificate chain and are published exactly as received. Their signatures belong to the authority, so they can be verified but never regenerated, and anchoring/v1/ is therefore immutable.
howTheseWereProduced.references: A receipt.token whose value begins with "@" names an entry in `receipts`. Every other string is literal. A case names its subject through `subjectRef`, an entry in `subjects`.
howTheseWereProduced.whatIsNotHere: Half two of the specification. Not one case in bindingCases or refusals establishes that a token is genuine: they check that a receipt is ABOUT a subject. The signature, the timestamping extended key usage, the certificate validity at genTime, the chain to a PINNED root and the policy are all unchecked by the reference implementation.
howTheseWereProduced.runtimeDivergence: bindingCases and refusals are the agreement points: every conformant runtime must behave identically on them. runtimeDivergence is the opposite — the one published case where a half-one implementation and a half-two implementation MUST differ, with what each must do. It is separate from bindingCases because calling it agreement would be a false claim about what half one establishes.
howTheseWereProduced.immutability: anchoring/v1/ is immutable exactly like a released schema directory, commitment/v1/, trust-registry/v1/ and evidence-log/v1/.

authority.note: Recorded so a reader can tell what produced these tokens. It is not an endorsement, a default, or a statement that any deployment uses this authority: the pinned roots and admissible policies are a verifier configuration, never part of this contract.

bindingCases.description: a signed checkpoint witnessed by a real public timestamp authority: the imprint the subject and blinding nonce produce is the imprint inside the token, and the token answers the request the record names
a signed trust-registry document witnessed under the other domain tag, over { manifest, signatures } — the attestations the receipt itself lands in are excluded

the same anchor checked against the whole published document rather than the subject pair: attestations are dropped on the way in, so a document that has since GAINED a witness still verifies against the anchor it gained

runtimeDivergence.description: THE BOUNDARY, PUBLISHED AS A VECTOR: a token whose signature bytes were altered still BINDS — the messageImprint is untouched, so half one has nothing to object to. An implementation that performs half one only accepts it, and is therefore not a verifier. An implementation that performs half two MUST refuse it. Both behaviours are conformant; accepting it while calling the result verification is not.

halfTwo.note: ANCHOR_SIGNATURE_INVALID is the accurate code and the one to prefer. ANCHOR_RECEIPT_MALFORMED is permitted because some platforms verify the CMS signature inside the token DECODER — .NET Rfc3161TimestampToken.TryDecode returns false for a bad signature — so a runtime built on such a decoder cannot separate "unreadable" from "not genuine" without decoding twice. It must still refuse; only the code may differ.

refusals.description: a record declaring an anchoring version this implementation does not speak
a record with no version at all — refused as an unknown version before the member set is examined, never as a malformed record
a record carrying a member the closed set does not define
a record missing a required member
a status outside the closed set
a subject kind this format does not anchor — a per-record anchor, for instance
a blinding nonce of 31 bytes; the width is exactly 32 and is what makes the header unambiguous
a blinding nonce that is not canonical unpadded base64url
a request nonce shorter than the minimum this format carries
a record claiming ANCHORED while carrying no receipt
a PENDING record carrying a receipt — incoherent rather than helpful: it invites a reader to conclude from the receipt what the status denies
a receipt of a kind this version does not define
a record naming one origin while the subject it is checked against is from another — without this check a record could point every lookup at the wrong subject
a record naming one subject version while the subject document is another
an anchor that has not been witnessed yet. A subject without a witnessed anchor is never fully verified — a pending anchor is not a weaker anchor, it is no anchor
an anchor whose attempt failed, presented where an anchor was required
the right subject and the right token under the wrong blinding nonce. The nonce is part of the imprint, so it cannot be replaced after the fact
the checkpoint token presented as the registry anchor. Both were witnessed by the same authority seconds apart; the domain tags and the subjects still keep them apart
a subject whose bytes were altered after it was witnessed — a checkpoint claiming a larger tree than the one that was anchored
a token that answers a different request than the record names — what a replayed response looks like

a real token from the same authority whose messageImprint is SHA-512. The format defines one digest suite, and a suite it does not define is a refusal rather than a silent success on an imprint nobody compared
a token cut short — a value extends past the end of the token
a token whose contentType was altered: the bytes no longer say they are a CMS SignedData, so there is nothing here this implementation can claim to have read
a receipt token that is not base64 at all
